column1: # binaries.tsv — tools installed as prebuilt binaries into ~/bin.
#   name        make target + default binary name
#   owner/repo  GitHub repo whose *latest* release is queried. A three-part
#               host's API instead — same JSON, same regex matching.
#   asset-regex extended regex matched against each asset's download URL
#   bins        space-separated binaries to pull out (defaults to <name>)
# Built for x86_64 Linux. Edit a regex here to change arch or pin behaviour.
# When a regex matches both a musl and a glibc asset, the musl one wins (it's
# static, so it runs on any glibc). Write a gnu-only regex to override that.
# duckdb also ships a -musl asset, but it's *dynamically* linked against musl
# (loader /lib/ld-musl-x86_64.so.1), so it dies with "No such file or directory"
# on a glibc box. The musl-preference above would pick it — match glibc only.
# trippy installs the `trip` command. Its Rust musl build is static, so musl is safe.
# tt ships a raw (uncompressed) static Go binary called tt-linux; it lands in
# ~/bin as `tt`. Anchor the regex so it can't match tt-linux_arm/_arm64.
# ttyper publishes musl assets only for aarch64/i686, so x86_64 has to take the
# gnu build. It's safe: the binary needs nothing newer than GLIBC_2.18.
# gh is the GitHub CLI. Upstream ships a static Go binary inside a tarball that
# unpacks to gh_<ver>_linux_amd64/bin/gh — a nested layout _find_bin resolves by
# the amd64 in the path. The $ anchor keeps the regex off the .deb and .rpm
# siblings of the same name, which this framework has no unpacker for.
# tea is the Gitea CLI, and Gitea does not develop it on GitHub: go-gitea/tea is
# an archived mirror that publishes no releases, so this row uses the
# host/owner/repo form above to query gitea.com's own API. Upstream's advice is
# the prebuilt binary; the linux-amd64 asset is a static Go binary (29 MB), and
# the $ anchor keeps the regex off its .xz and .xz.sha256 siblings, which this
# framework has no unpacker for (plain .xz is not a tarball).
